title: Grilled Corn on the Cob
subtitle: BBQ-charred corn with seasoned butter
excerpt: Corn on the cob grilled directly over heat picks up char and sweetness that boiled corn doesn't. The husk is removed before grilling so the kernels directly contact the heat and colour. A seasoned compound butter, chilli, lime, coriander, goes on as it comes off the grill.
sourceNotes: Grilled corn on the cob is one of the central dishes of the American cookout. The compound butter finish is modelled on the Mexican elotes preparation, which became widely adopted across American BBQ culture.

recipe.batchNotes: Scales easily on a grill; make as many as you can fit.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the butter ahead. Keep in the fridge for up to a week.

content.text: Grilled corn is one of the simplest things you can cook outdoors and one of the best. The kernels char slightly at high heat and the sugars caramelise, giving a sweetness and complexity that boiled corn entirely lacks. This version uses a chilli-lime butter as the finish, simple and very good.
No outdoor grill? Use a cast-iron griddle pan on the hob over high heat. Turn the corn frequently to char on all sides. The result is slightly less smoky but the caramelisation is similar.

items.prepNote: to coat the corn before grilling

content.text: Make the butter and grill the corn

Mash together {{unsalted-butter}}, the zest and juice of {{lime}}, {{chilli-flakes}}, {{garlic-powder}}, {{fresh-coriander}} if using, and {{sea-salt-fine}} until combined. Roll the mixture into a log in cling film and refrigerate while you cook the corn.

Brush {{sweetcorn-cob}} all over with {{rapeseed-oil}} and season with {{sea-salt-flakes}}. Place on a preheated grill or very hot griddle pan. Cook for 10 to 15 minutes, turning every two to three minutes, until the corn has char marks on all sides and smells sweet and smoky.
Remove the corn from the heat and immediately rub generously with slices of the chilli-lime butter. Serve straight away, the butter melts over the hot corn as it sits.

items.symptom: The corn is charred on the outside but raw in the middle
items.cause: Heat too high or corn didn't get turned enough.
items.fix: Fresh corn cooks quickly at 10 to 15 minutes over moderate direct heat with frequent turning. If the corn is charring too fast before cooking through, move it to indirect heat on a BBQ and close the lid.

items.symptom: The kernels are tough and starchy, not sweet
items.cause: Corn past its best, or stored too long before cooking.
items.fix: Fresh sweetcorn is best used within two to three days of picking. The sugars convert to starch quickly. The sweetest corn is bought from a farm shop rather than a supermarket.

items.symptom: The butter doesn't melt into the corn
items.cause: Corn not hot enough, or butter too cold from the fridge.
items.fix: Add the butter immediately when the corn comes off the heat. The surface should be hot enough to melt the butter within 30 seconds.

items.symptom: The corn sticks to the griddle
items.cause: Not enough oil, or griddle not hot enough before the corn goes on.
items.fix: The griddle must be smoking hot before the corn goes on. Coat the corn evenly in oil. Don't try to move it until char marks have formed and it releases naturally.

content.text: Corn on the cob is one of the oldest foods in America, grown by indigenous peoples for thousands of years. Grilling corn over fire is a traditional preparation in many Native American food cultures. The compound butter finish draws on Mexican elotes: corn dressed with butter, lime, chilli, and cheese. This has had a strong influence on American BBQ culture, especially in Texas and the Southwest.
